text: A base table is a foundational table ServiceNow ships with that's deliberately generic, built to hold the fields and behavior that many more specific record types all need, without committing to any one of them. Task is the base table behind Incident, Problem, Change, and Request management. Cmdb_ci is the base table behind every configuration item type in the CMDB — a server, a database instance, a network switch. Neither is meant to be used directly very often.

Table extension is the mechanism that lets one table build on another, and it's real inheritance, not a copy-paste. Incident's Extends table field, in sys_db_object, points to task. That single relationship means incident automatically inherits every field task has — short description, state, priority, assignment group, and dozens more — without one of those fields being redefined on incident itself. Incident then adds its own fields on top: caller_id, category, close_code, fields that only make sense on an incident.

Problem and change_request extend task the exact same way, each adding fields specific to its own purpose. Problem adds known_error and workaround, fields that only matter during root-cause investigation. Change_request adds risk, type, and backout_plan, fields that only matter when you're planning a controlled change. ServiceNow's modern extension pattern gives each of these its own physical table under the hood, while still presenting inherited fields as if they live right there on the child's form.

Because incident extends task, every incident record is simultaneously a row that satisfies a query against task. Build a report or list against task with no further filtering, and ServiceNow returns incidents, problems, change requests, and service catalog requests all mixed together — because every one of them is a task, just dressed up with its own extra fields. That's exactly how a manager's single all-open-work dashboard can exist without separately querying four tables by hand.

This is precisely why Incident, Problem, and Change Management, the ITIL practices from your first course in this path, behave so consistently with each other: the same state field, the same assignment_group field, the same priority calculation logic all live once on task and get inherited everywhere. Learn how one shared behavior works on Incident, and you've learned how it works on Problem and Change too. Next up: mapping the real task table hierarchy.
